data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories in action is defensible without smuggling induction by reframing 'preference' as a methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests, not as an inductive bet on truth or reliability; the cost is accepting that acting on a theory offers no rational guarantee of success, only the best available opportunity to learn quickly if we are wrong.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a probabilistic guarantee of safety (e.g., building a bridge where failure means death), this non-inductive preference is insufficient because it explicitly denies that past survival increases future reliability probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'acting on' implies relying on the theory's truth rather than its testability, the defense collapses into the very induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd-Miller critique of verisimilitude holds that we cannot logically compare the truth-content of false theories, then 'better-corroborated' loses its objective ranking power for action.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Severe Test Maximization': choosing the theory with the highest corroboration means choosing the one that has survived the most stringent attempts at falsification. By acting on it, we subject our practical endeavors to the sharpest possible knife-edge; if the theory is false, the high-stakes application will likely reveal the error faster and more dramatically than applying a less-tested theory, thereby accelerating the growth of knowledge even in the realm of action.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
